opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what strikes me most is that it was possible at all. When people think about training something in the tens of billions of parameters, they usually picture a big industry lab with a dedicated team and a cluster tuned specifically for that one job. We're a fairly small academic group, and we had an allocation on a research supercomputer that wasn't built with large language model training as its primary use case.

The trick is that our model doesn't actually have 32 billion parameters. It's a recurrent-depth architecture. There's a relatively small core block that we loop over many times, so the parameter count stays modest, but the compute per token, in FLOPs, can match a much larger fixed-depth model. That makes things very different practically. The memory footprint is that of a small model, so you don't need the heavy sharding and model parallelism that make large runs fragile. You're mostly doing data parallelism at scale, which is much more forgiving, especially on hardware where the software stack is less mature than the standard NVIDIA setup.

It wasn't free, though. Getting stable training on that system took a lot of debugging. We had communication issues, numerical stability problems, and a few early runs where the recurrence just collapsed and the model learned to ignore the extra iterations. Each of those failures cost real compute. But once it worked, it showed that if you're clever about where the compute goes, by putting it into depth and iteration instead of raw parameters, you can do work in academia that looks out of reach on paper.

For me it also reframes the question. People ask how many parameters you can afford, but a better question is how much computation you want the model to do and where you want it to happen. Recurrence lets you decouple those, and it lets the model choose to think longer at test time on harder problems. That's the part I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the smaller model’s memory footprint and reduced need for sharding, but does not attribute the cluster’s inability to train a FLOP-equivalent 32-billion-parameter model to the amount of state transferred between devices.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that really struck me, honestly, is that it was feasible at all on our hardware. We're an academic lab, so we don't have anything like a hyperscaler cluster. And the model that comes out of the recurrent-depth training, if you count the compute that actually goes through it, it's behaving like a 32 billion parameter model in terms of FLOPs per token. But the actual number of parameters we have to store and move around is far smaller, around 3.5 billion. So what we're really doing is trading parameters for compute.

That matters a lot practically. The dominant costs in training at this scale, on a cluster like ours, are communication and memory. If you have a 32 billion parameter dense model, you need to shard it, you need big optimizer states, you spend a huge amount of time moving gradients between devices. With the recurrent model, the parameter footprint is small enough that it fits comfortably, and the communication overhead is the same as for a small model, while the compute per token is large. And compute is the thing a GPU is actually good at. So the hardware was being used in a way that matched its strengths, which is not usually the case when you try to train large dense models with limited interconnect.

The other thing I found striking is more conceptual. We went into this not knowing whether a model that just loops a block of layers would train stably at scale, or whether it would learn anything that a shallow model couldn't. And it did. It picks up behaviors like doing more iterations on harder tokens, and the performance improves as you give it more recurrence at test time. So the feasibility isn't just "we could afford the run." It's that this kind of architecture actually works out when you scale it, and it does so on compute that a university group can get access to. That was not obvious to us at the start.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a dense 32B model would require sharding and moving gradients between devices, creating heavy communication overhead that limited interconnect makes impractical on their cluster.

astra-6.text: What I find striking is that, from a compute perspective, it’s within reach. You hear “32 billion parameters” and assume that’s something only a large industrial lab can train. But if you look at the FLOP budget, you can start to imagine doing it on our cluster. Of course, FLOP-equivalent doesn’t mean equally easy to train—you still have to fit the model, move data between devices, and keep the hardware busy. But it makes the question very concrete: how much of that theoretical compute can we actually turn into useful training?

sol-6.1.text: What’s striking to me is that it’s actually feasible at all. A 32 billion parameter model sounds like something that should require an enormous industrial cluster, but if you look at an equivalent training budget in FLOPs, it starts to look achievable on the hardware we have. That doesn’t mean it’s easy, or that FLOP equivalence guarantees the same model quality. You still have to make the whole system work efficiently. But it changes the question from “Could we possibly do this?” to “What’s the best experiment we can run with that compute?”
